title: What a $50 course really costs
hook: The price tag says $50. Is that all you pay?

doesNotKnow: that the cost of a choice includes the best alternative given up
that given-up earnings count only if the alternative was really available

objective: The learner can explain that the cost of a choice is what is given up to make it, including time that could have been paid, and that this part vanishes when there was no paid alternative.

claims.text: A $50 course that takes 3 hours, when you could have earned $20 an hour, costs you $110: the $50 fee plus $60 of pay given up.
The cost of a choice is what you give up to make it, and time is one of the things given up.
claims.source: Opportunity cost: 'the cost of something is what you give up to get it' (N. G. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 1, Ten Principles, principle 2).

claims.text: If no paid work was available in those hours, the given-up pay is $0 and the course costs only its $50 fee.
claims.source: The opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative actually available; with no paid alternative that value is 0 in this model, so cost(h, false) = 50 for every h.

claims.text: On the stage the real cost is $50 + $20 × hours, from $70 at 1 hour to $210 at 8 hours.
The numbers are a toy model: it assumes the $20-an-hour work was on offer and ignores taxes and the value of what the course teaches.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation (Demo.tsx), shown on the stage chip and in the reveal.

recall.question: A free concert takes 4 hours. You could have tutored for $15 an hour instead. What did the concert cost you?
recall.why: The cost of a choice is what you give up. Four hours of tutoring at $15 is $60 given up, even though the ticket was free.
